gloss: be new, renew; new; new moon, month
summary: חדש is newness: חָדָשׁ is what has not been before or not been used (a new cart, a new king, the new grain of Lev 23:16), and the piel חִדֵּשׁ makes a thing new again, restoring what was worn or broken. חֹדֶשׁ is the moon’s renewing, the day the new crescent appears, kept with offerings and the shofar, and from it the month, counted from one new moon to the next; every date of Lev 23 is a day “of the חֹדֶשׁ”. The prophets take the adjective up for what Yahweh will do: a new song, a new heart and spirit, a new covenant, new heavens and a new earth, and the New Testament quotes them. Arabic ḥaduṯa “be new”, Ugaritic ḥdṯ “new moon” and Aramaic חֲדַת show the root’s older consonants ḥ-d-ṯ: its ש is an old ṯ.

words.gloss: new moon, the moon’s renewing; month
words.summary: First the day of the new moon, then the month that runs from it to the next. Ugaritic ḥdṯ and Phoenician ḥdš are the new moon only (Phoenician never uses it for “month”), so the month sense is the Hebrew’s own extension.

senses.definition: New, of timber for the rebuilt house of God, in its one use.

senses.definition: New, against old: new cloth and new wine, the new covenant, a new commandment, the new creation and new man, the new heaven and earth.

cognates.gloss: be new, come newly into being; (III) polish a sword, as though making it new
cognates.note: Arabic ح (ḥ, not خ ḫ) and ث (ṯ, not ش š). Form III, polishing a sword “as though he made it new”, stands near the piel “restore”. Arabic’s “tell, relate” (حَدَّثَ, حَدِيث “news, story”) is its own development from the new thing reported and has no Hebrew counterpart.

evidence.note: “It was new, or recent; contr. of قَدُمَ … it (a thing) came into existence … existed newly, for the first time, not having been before.”
“He polished his sword; [as though he made it new by doing so].”
“New, recent; contr. of قَدِيمٌ [old].”

cognates.note: Ugaritic keeps ḥ and ḫ, and ṯ and š, apart; this word has ḥ and ṯ. Segert vocalises /ḥudṯ-/, the Hebrew noun’s pattern.

evidence.note: “/ḥudṯ-/ “new moon” (H. ḥódæš < *ḥudṯ-)”. Page image read (leaf n212).

cognates.note: Dated inscriptions read “on the new moon of the month (yrḥ) of Ethanim”; Krahmalkov notes ḥdš is never a synonym of yrḥ “month” in Phoenician-Punic, so the month sense of חֹדֶשׁ is not shared. Phoenician script cannot show ḥ/ḫ or ṯ/š.

evidence.note: “[Heb. ḥodeš] n.m. NEW MOON”; “So, too, did I make sacrifice monthly on the new moons and on the full moons”; “Obs. In Phoenician-Punic, ḥdš is never a synonym of yrḥ, month.”
“[Heb. ḥadaš] adj. 1. NEW”: “new sanctuaries”, the New Gate; “2. NEWBORN”.

cognates.note: The same stem and sense as the Hebrew piel of 2Ch 24:4.

evidence.note: “[Heb. ḥ-d-š] v. piʿel 1. RESTORE, RENOVATE … He restored and dedicated the broken cattle-altar”; “2. Expressing prefix re- … rebuilt these three sanctuaries”.

cognates.note: Akkadian loses ḥ (leaving e-colouring, as here) but keeps ḫ, so edēšu fits an older ḥ; it cannot show ṯ from š.

evidence.note: Meanings include be renewed, be(come) restored, renew, renovate.
Meanings: fresh; new; new (one).

doctrine.statement: Yahweh promises “a new covenant (בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה) with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant I made with their fathers” when he took them out of Egypt, which they broke: he will put his law within them and write it on their heart, they will all know him, and he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more (Jer 31:31–34). At the last supper Jesus takes the cup and says, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you” (Luk 22:20; 1Co 11:25). Hebrews quotes Jer 31:31–34 in full and draws from the one word “new” that the first covenant is made old, and what grows old is near to vanishing (Heb 8:8–13); Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant, by his death for the transgressions under the first (Heb 9:15; 12:24), and Paul calls the apostles ministers of a new covenant, of the spirit and not the letter (2Co 3:6).

Israel is told, “make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit; why will you die?” (Ezk 18:31), and Yahweh promises to do it: “a new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you; I will remove the heart of stone … and give you a heart of flesh”, his spirit within them so that they walk in his statutes (Ezk 36:26–27; 11:19). David prays, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew (חַדֵּשׁ) a steadfast spirit within me” (Psa 51:12). The apostles write of the same work in those who are in Christ: he is a new creation, the old has passed, all is new (2Co 5:17); be renewed in the spirit of your mind and put on the new man, created after God in righteousness and holiness (Eph 4:23–24; Col 3:10); be transformed by the renewing of your mind (Rom 12:2); though the outer man wastes away, the inner is renewed day by day (2Co 4:16). The Peshitta uses this root throughout (ܚܕܬ). God gives the new heart; the one who receives it is to make it his own and walk in it.

A new song is sung to Yahweh for a new act of his: “he drew me up from the pit … he put a new song in my mouth” (Psa 40:3–4); “sing to Yahweh a new song, for he has done marvellous things; his right hand has saved him” (Psa 98:1); and among the nations, because he comes to judge the earth in righteousness (Psa 96:1, 13; Isa 42:9–10). In Revelation the living creatures and elders sing a new song to the Lamb: “you are worthy … for you were slain, and redeemed us to God by your blood out of every tribe, … and made us kings and priests to our God, and we shall reign on the earth”, and only the redeemed can learn the new song before the throne (Rev 5:9–10; 14:3).

“Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things will not be remembered” (Isa 65:17). Isaiah describes what that creating is: Jerusalem created a rejoicing and her people a joy, no more weeping in her, long life, houses built and lived in, vineyards planted and eaten from, wolf and lamb feeding together, no harm in all Yahweh’s holy mountain (Isa 65:18–25). As the new heavens and earth remain before him, so Israel’s seed and name remain, and from new moon to new moon and sabbath to sabbath all flesh comes to worship before him (Isa 66:22–23). Peter, “according to his promise”, looks for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2Pe 3:13), and John sees them, with the holy city, new Jerusalem, God dwelling with men, death and mourning gone, and hears, “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev 21:1–5).

The new moon was a day of burnt offerings and trumpets over them, “a memorial before your God” (Num 10:10; 28:11–15), and Lev 23:24 makes the seventh new moon a rest and a memorial of shouting. Kept without righteousness it was hateful to Yahweh (Isa 1:13–14), and he said he would make Israel’s new moons cease (Hos 2:13). Paul tells the Colossians: “let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast, or a new moon, or sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:16–17). The prophets also see new moons in the age to come, the east gate of the house opened on the day of the new moon and all flesh worshipping before Yahweh from new moon to new moon (Ezk 46:1, 3; Isa 66:23).

note: Left out for name entries: חֹדֶשׁ Hodesh, a woman (BDB h.aw.ad, 1Ch 8:9), חֲדָשָׁה Hadashah (h.aw.ae, Jos 15:37), חָדְשִׁי in תַּחְתִּים חָדְשִׁי (h.aw.af, 2Sa 24:6), and חָצוֹר חֲדַתָּה (Jos 15:25). BDB’s h.aw.ad key is matched in the database to 44 tokens, nearly all ordinary “month/new moon” tokens (Gen 29:14, Num 3:15 …) that are also under h.aw.ac; only 1Ch 8:9 is the name, so h.aw.ad is not put on the noun. The month in Aramaic (Biblical and Peshitta) is יְרַח/ܝܪܚܐ, another root, so this entry has no Aramaic “month”; Col 2:16’s Peshitta “new moon” is ܪܝܫ ܝܪܚܐ, not this root. Sounds: Arabic and Ugaritic both show ḥ (not ḫ) and ṯ (not š); Aramaic ת (חֲדַת, ܚܕܬ) agrees with ṯ. Checked: Lane pp. 527–529; Segert p. 185 on the page image (leaf n212); Krahmalkov pp. 177–178 from the local PDF’s text layer only (page not seen as an image: no renderer); Oracc edēšu, eššu. Segert’s grammar also cites bym ḥdṯ “on the day of the new moon” (OCR reads KTU 1.105:1, §81.3; page not identified or seen), not entered. Not consulted: Ge’ez ḥaddasa (Dillmann, Leslau; Wiktionary lead only), Sabaic ḥdṯ, CAD. Open: (1) Jastrow glosses חָדַשׁ “[to be bright,] to be new”, implying the moon’s brightness as the root’s first sense; no evidence followed, and the cognates point to “new”. (2) The Peshitta lemma pointings follow SEDRA’s forms; SEDRA lexeme 968 חוּדָּתָא (Jhn 10:22 “Dedication”) is the feast called חֲנֻכָּה in later Hebrew, which is not in scripture. (3) Eph 1:10: the Peshitta’s “be renewed” renders Greek “sum up”; kept as the Peshitta’s use. (4) Lev 23:16 מִנְחָה חֲדָשָׁה is “new” in the plain sense, the first grain of the new harvest; the NT has no quotation of it, so νέος cites only Heb 12:24 (the new covenant).
